questions.question: A tool reads a photo of a restaurant menu and answers the question "Which dishes are vegetarian?" in text. Which model family is most likely involved?
options: A diffusion model, because the input is an image.
A predictive model, because it gives a label to each dish.
A multimodal model, because it takes in an image and produces text.
A language model only, because the answer is written in text.
questions.explanation: The tool takes in one type of data (an image) and produces another (text), which is what multimodal models do. The most tempting wrong option is "a language model only". A text-only language model cannot read the photo; the ability to take in the image is what makes it multimodal.

questions.question: How does a large language model produce a long answer?
options: It predicts the next token, adds it to the text, and repeats this many times.
It finds a complete answer in a stored database and copies it.
It plans the full answer in advance and then types it out word by word.
It searches the internet for every sentence it writes.
questions.explanation: A language model builds its answer one token at a time, each time predicting a likely next token from all the text so far. The most tempting wrong option is that it plans the full answer first. It does not write from a finished plan, which is why a small change in the prompt or temperature can change the direction of the answer.

questions.question: Ines needs a model to extract dates from invoices in the same way every time. Which temperature setting should she choose?
options: A high temperature, so the model can be more creative.
A high temperature, so the model reads more of the invoice.
Temperature does not matter for this kind of task.
A low temperature, so the model gives more predictable, consistent answers.
questions.explanation: A low temperature makes the model choose the most likely tokens almost every time, which gives consistent results for tasks like extraction. The most tempting wrong option is a high temperature for creativity. Creativity and variety are useful for brainstorming, but for data extraction they only add the risk of different or invented answers.

questions.question: In the simplified training picture, which stage mainly teaches a model to behave like a helpful assistant that answers questions and follows instructions?
options: Pre-training on a very large collection of text.
Fine-tuning on examples of good requests and answers.
The user's conversation, which trains the model in real time.
The context window, which stores the rules of good behaviour.
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning uses carefully prepared examples of requests and helpful answers, so the model learns the format and behaviour of an assistant. The most tempting wrong option is pre-training. Pre-training gives general language skills and knowledge, but a pre-trained model is good at continuing text, not yet at acting as a helpful assistant.

questions.question: Arjun gives a chatbot his team's leave policy and asks about a rule the policy does not mention. The chatbot answers with a clear, specific rule. What is the best description of this answer?
options: A context window error, because the policy was too long to read.
A correct answer from the model's training data.
A hallucination: a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by the source.
A knowledge cut-off, because the policy is newer than the model.
questions.explanation: The model generated a likely-sounding rule that is not in the policy, which is a hallucination. The most tempting wrong option is the knowledge cut-off. The cut-off explains why a model does not know recent events, but here the source was given to the model; the problem is that it invented an answer instead of saying "not stated".
